opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this started almost as a personal habit. When you train a lot of models, especially small ones where you can run many experiments, you start staring at loss curves all day. At some point I began playing a little game with myself: before a run finished, I would look at the first few hundred steps and try to guess what the curve would do next. Will it plateau? Will there be a sudden drop, like a grokking-style phase transition? Will it diverge?

At first I was pretty bad at it. But after doing it hundreds of times, I noticed I was getting better. I developed intuitions: "this kind of slow descent with a bit of noise usually means the learning rate is a bit too small," or "this little bump often comes right before the model discovers some structure." These weren't things I could write down as theorems. They were more like the intuition an experienced chef has about when the food is done.

That made me realize two things. First, a lot of what we call "research taste" in deep learning is really pattern recognition over training dynamics. Second, pattern recognition is exactly what neural networks are good at. If I, as a human, could learn to predict training curves just by watching enough of them, a model could probably learn to do it too, and probably better, because it can look at far more runs than I ever could.

So the natural question became: why are humans still the ones babysitting training runs, tuning hyperparameters, and deciding which experiment to try next? That's the core of what I mean by AI for AI: using AI systems to understand, predict, and eventually help design the training of other AI systems. It's a kind of science of AI where the scientist itself can be partially automated.

I also think there's a deeper motivation. As models get bigger, each training run gets more expensive, and we can't afford to just try things. If you could predict from a small-scale or early-stage run how a large run will behave, that saves enormous compute. And it pushes us toward a more physics-like understanding: finding the regularities and "laws" of training, rather than treating it as alchemy.

So it really started with a silly guessing game, but it changed how I think about where research in this field could go.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he repeatedly guessed what curves would do before runs finished and improved after doing this hundreds of times.

r002.rationale: It does not describe his curve-prediction ability transferring across domains such as language and vision.

fable-5.1.text:
Ziming Liu: It actually started as a kind of game I played with myself. When I was training models, I'd stare at the loss curve and try to guess what would happen next. Will this plateau? Is this the beginning of grokking, where the training loss has gone down but the test loss is still flat and then suddenly drops? Will the loss spike and recover, or will it diverge? At first I was wrong all the time. But over months, I started to develop intuition. I could look at the first few hundred steps and say, this run is going to be fine, or this learning rate is too high, you'll see it blow up around step two thousand.

And then I asked myself a strange question. Why can I do this? What am I actually doing when I predict a training curve? I'm looking at patterns in the data, I'm comparing to many past runs I've seen, I'm forming a hypothesis and checking it. That's not magic. That's exactly what a machine learning model does. So if I, with a very limited memory and a very slow brain, can learn to predict training dynamics, then a model with access to thousands or millions of training runs should be able to do it far better.

That was the moment the idea of AI for AI crystallized for me. We spend enormous resources on training large models, and most of the decisions, the learning rate schedule, when to stop, which architecture variant to try, are still made by human intuition, which is really just slow pattern matching on limited experience. Why not make that pattern matching explicit and let a model do it? A model that reads training curves, predicts outcomes, and suggests interventions. Essentially, use machine learning to study machine learning itself.

I also think there's a deeper point here. Physics was my background, and in physics you have this tradition of building a theory from observations of phenomena. Training dynamics are phenomena. Grokking is a phenomenon, loss spikes are phenomena, scaling laws are phenomena. Right now we mostly describe them, like naturalists collecting specimens. AI for AI, to me, is trying to move from the collecting stage to the predictive stage, where we actually have a model, maybe a learned one, maybe a mechanistic one, that tells us what will happen before we spend the compute. And predicting the curve with my own eyes was just the first, very primitive version of that.

astra-6.text:
For me, the connection was learning to think of AI research itself as a prediction problem. When you look at an early training curve, you’re asking: Will this run improve? Has it plateaued? Is it worth spending more compute on it? Training yourself to make those predictions means forming hypotheses and then checking them against what actually happens.

That led me to ask: could a model learn to make those judgments too? The training curve is just one piece of evidence. You could also give it the experimental setup and the results of previous runs, and ask it to suggest what to try next.

That’s the idea of AI for AI: using AI to help with the process of developing AI. Predicting a curve is a fairly narrow starting point, but it points toward a larger loop—propose an experiment, run it, interpret the result, and use that result to choose the next experiment.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the connection was that predicting training curves is itself a learning problem. You look at the early part of a run and try to predict where it will end up. As you practice, you develop intuitions about which signals matter and which changes might help.

Then the natural question is: if I can learn to do this, could a model learn to do it too? And if it can predict the outcome of an experiment, could it also help choose the next experiment?

That’s the connection to AI for AI: using AI to improve the process of developing AI. Predicting a training curve is a concrete starting point, but the broader idea is to build a feedback loop where a system proposes experiments, learns from the results, and gets better at deciding what to try next.
